shared_context.patient: a 1-year-old girl with increasing seizure frequency over the past 2 months.

atoms.1: Hypsarrhythmia is a characteristic pattern seen in infantile spasms (West syndrome).
atoms.2: These episodes are consistent with infantile spasms.
atoms.3: The combination of hypopigmented macules and an elevated plaque on the back suggests a diagnosis of Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC).
atoms.4: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC) is a genetic disorder.
atoms.5: TSC causes benign tumors to form in many different organs, primarily the brain, skin, kidneys, heart, eyes, and lungs.
atoms.6: Key skin manifestations of TSC include hypopigmented macules (ash-leaf spots) and Shagreen patches (thickened, elevated plaques).
atoms.7: Key neurological manifestations of TSC include infantile spasms and hypsarrhythmia on EEG.
atoms.8: Key cardiac manifestations of TSC include the presence of cardiac rhabdomyomas.
atoms.9: Cardiac rhabdomyomas are benign tumors of the heart.
atoms.10: Cardiac rhabdomyomas are commonly associated with TSC.
atoms.11: Cardiac rhabdomyomas can be detected at any age, often during infancy.
atoms.12: Glaucoma is associated with other conditions, not typically linked to TSC.
atoms.13: Optic glioma is more commonly associated with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).
atoms.14: Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia is associated with McCune-Albright syndrome.
atoms.15: Renal cell carcinoma is not typically linked to TSC.
atoms.16: TSC patients are at risk for renal angiomyolipomas and renal cell carcinoma in adulthood.
atoms.17: The clinical presentation of infantile spasms, hypsarrhythmia, hypopigmented macules, and Shagreen patch is most consistent with Tuberous Sclerosis Complex.
atoms.18: Cardiac rhabdomyomas are commonly found in TSC patients and serve as a strong association with this condition.

snippets.output: Hypsarrhythmia is a characteristic pattern seen in infantile spasms (West syndrome).
The episode where the patient stiffens and spreads her arms, is consistent with infantile spasms.
The combination of hypopigmented macules and an elevated plaque on the back suggests a diagnosis of Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC).
Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC) is a genetic disorder.
TSC causes benign tumors to form in many different organs, primarily the brain, skin, kidneys, heart, eyes, and lungs.
Key skin manifestations of TSC include hypopigmented macules (ash-leaf spots) and Shagreen patches (thickened, elevated plaques).
Key neurological manifestations of TSC include infantile spasms and hypsarrhythmia on EEG.
Key cardiac manifestations of TSC include the presence of cardiac rhabdomyomas.
Cardiac rhabdomyomas are benign tumors of the heart.
Cardiac rhabdomyomas are commonly associated with TSC.
Cardiac rhabdomyomas can be detected at any age, often during infancy.
Glaucoma is associated with other conditions, not typically linked to TSC.
Optic glioma is more commonly associated with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).
Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia is associated with McCune-Albright syndrome.
Renal cell carcinoma is not typically linked to TSC.
TSC patients are at risk for renal angiomyolipomas and renal cell carcinoma in adulthood.
The clinical presentation of infantile spasms, hypsarrhythmia, hypopigmented macules, and Shagreen patch is most consistent with Tuberous Sclerosis Complex.
Cardiac rhabdomyomas are commonly found in TSC patients and serve as a strong association with this condition.
